Request.theme: warehouse inventory diversion with badge records and file metadata

Metadata.title: The Missing Pallet Ledger
Metadata.description: A mid-size fulfillment warehouse reports a quiet inventory diversion masked as routine cycle counts. Badge access logs and file metadata suggest someone used ordinary systems and a small procedural gap to walk product out.
Metadata.briefing: Overnight counts at a Daly City warehouse don’t reconcile, but the paperwork looks clean. Your job is to determine whether it’s error or diversion—and who used routine access controls to make it happen.

Blueprint.crimeMechanism: Linh Tran used after-hours badge access to enter the office mezzanine and log into a shared workstation that was left signed in to a generic warehouse reporting account. She exported a pick-face variance report, edited the cycle-count adjustment spreadsheet to reclassify a pallet of high-value handheld scanners as 'damaged/returns' and reduce on-hand counts, then submitted the adjustment via the WMS before the 04:00 auto-post window. She then used a legitimate dock-side 'returns cage' process to move the pallet to an area where outbound carriers don’t require a standard bill of lading scan, and arranged a same-day pickup under a small local courier account. Concealment relied on ordinary process gaps: generic account sessions, routine cycle-count variance edits, and a returns-cage exception lane with weaker paperwork requirements.
Blueprint.culpritObjective: She needed one pallet of handheld scanners diverted before the quarterly inventory audit pre-count began the next evening, when tighter controls and supervised counts would have made adjustments conspicuous; the theft was timed to exploit the last low-scrutiny overnight window.
Blueprint.caseHook: The only anomaly at opening is that the cycle-count spreadsheet looks properly approved, yet its file metadata shows it was edited after the approval time—during an after-hours badge entry.

incidentSequence.event: Linh Tran badged into the warehouse employee entrance and proceeded to the office mezzanine.
incidentSequence.publicDescription: After-hours badge access records show an employee entered through the staff entrance at 02:41.

incidentSequence.event: Using a mezzanine workstation already authenticated to the generic reporting account, Linh generated/exported the variance report and opened the cycle-count adjustment spreadsheet.
Linh edited the cycle-count adjustment spreadsheet entries for a specific pallet of handheld scanners to move it into 'damaged/returns' disposition and reduce on-hand totals.
incidentSequence.publicDescription: The cycle-count adjustment spreadsheet shows edits during the 03:00 hour despite appearing approved.

incidentSequence.event: The WMS accepted and posted the adjustment batch, making the on-hand totals match the altered spreadsheet.
incidentSequence.publicDescription: The WMS shows an adjustment batch posted at 03:12 that changed on-hand counts for the affected SKU.

incidentSequence.event: Linh used the returns-cage exception lane to move the pallet into the outbound returns staging area without a standard outbound shipment scan.
Day shift noticed the pallet location empty and escalated to management when the cycle-count paperwork did not match physical staging expectations.
incidentSequence.publicDescription: At 09:47, day shift reported a high-value pallet location empty and requested a reconciliation review.

clueLadder.discovery: A reconciliation email thread dated 2026-03-18 references SKU HHS-4102 'handheld scanners' showing a -48 unit variance after the 03:12 adjustment batch.
clueLadder.inference: The case centers on a specific high-value SKU and a narrow overnight adjustment window rather than broad shrink.

clueLadder.discovery: Badge log entry 'TRN-L' shows badge ID 004982 opened Door E-Staff at 2026-03-18 02:41:18 and Door MZ-Office at 2026-03-18 02:49:02.
clueLadder.inference: Badge ID 004982 had after-hours access to the office mezzanine where reporting and adjustment documents are typically handled.

clueLadder.discovery: WMS audit log shows adjustment batch 'ADJ-20260318-0312' posted at 2026-03-18 03:12:00 and initiated by user 'rpt-floor' from terminal name 'MZ-PC-03'.
clueLadder.inference: A specific batch and opaque initiator identity (user/terminal) exist that can be traced independently of badge records.

clueLadder.discovery: The spreadsheet 'CycleCount_Adjustments_2026-03-18.xlsx' on the shared drive shows 'Last Modified: 2026-03-18 03:06:44' and 'Last Modified By: LINH.T' in its file properties.
clueLadder.inference: The adjustment document was edited at a time consistent with the overnight activity and by a specific account identity that can be cross-checked against system actions.

clueLadder.discovery: Forensic analysis of MZ-PC-03 shows Windows Event Log entry 'Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing 4624' with Logon ID 0x3F2A9 for user LINH.T at 2026-03-18 02:54:58 and WMS client log line 'SessionToken=7c1b9a2e' at 2026-03-18 03:11:41 on the same machine.
clueLadder.inference: The workstation and WMS session token associated with the 03:12 batch can be tied to Linh's authenticated session on MZ-PC-03.

clueLadder.discovery: Gate log lists 'Bay 2 pickup' for courier 'Peninsula SameDay' at 2026-03-18 04:06 with reference 'RET-EXC-1187' and contact phone ending -5521.
clueLadder.inference: A physical removal event occurred shortly after the adjustment, consistent with an exception returns pathway rather than normal outbound shipping.

redHerrings.suspicion: As shipping supervisor, Owen could alter outbound paperwork or stage pallets to leave through the dock without scrutiny.
redHerrings.verification: BOL packet scan log shows Owen's supervisor login 'ODEL' recorded at Dock Office kiosk at 2026-03-18 08:14:22 and 08:37:05, with no entries between 01:00 and 06:00.
redHerrings.resolution: His recorded system activity starts well after the overnight adjustment and does not account for the after-hours office access or the 03:12 batch initiation.

redHerrings.suspicion: As inventory control lead, Maya's approval authority could allow her to legitimize an improper cycle-count adjustment.
redHerrings.verification: Email header on 'Re: Cycle Count 3/18 approvals' shows message-id <cc0318-approval@warehouse.local> sent from MAYA.K at 2026-03-18 01:22:09 with the attached spreadsheet hash 'SHA256 9b1d...e20f' differing from the shared drive file hash 'SHA256 4c7a...19d2' recorded at 2026-03-18 03:15:02 by the file server audit.
redHerrings.resolution: The approval email references an earlier attachment version, consistent with a later modification occurring after her approval rather than her authoring the final altered file.

redHerrings.suspicion: As the overnight guard, Rafael could wave through an unauthorized pickup or falsify the gate log.
redHerrings.verification: Security shift roster shows guard 'R. Ibarra' assigned 22:00–06:00 and a separate dock camera motion log lists activity at Gatehouse window at 2026-03-18 04:05–04:08 coinciding with the 'Peninsula SameDay' entry.
redHerrings.resolution: The records indicate he was present and logging a pickup, but they do not connect him to the internal WMS adjustment, mezzanine workstation activity, or file modifications.

SuspectFull.name: Linh Tran
SuspectFull.relationship: Internal systems support for inventory control and night shift operations
SuspectFull.motive: She was under pressure to avoid a damaging variance ahead of the quarterly pre-count and wanted one problematic high-value pallet to disappear from the numbers before tighter controls kicked in. The after-hours window offered a chance to “fix” the records without having to explain an exception during the audit prep.
SuspectFull.alibi: She says she was on-site after hours to troubleshoot reporting access for the generic warehouse reporting account and to prep templates, and that her badge entry can be confirmed by access control logs. She cannot provide an independent witness for her time at the mezzanine workstations, since she says she worked alone and communicated only via email/IM.
SuspectFull.background:
Maintains WMS report templates, shared drive permissions, and supports inventory reporting users, including night shift.
Has access to office mezzanine areas and is familiar with cycle-count variance workflows and how adjustment spreadsheets are handled.
Her role gives her routine reason to use shared workstations and interact with the generic reporting account used for warehouse reporting.

SuspectFull.name: Maya Kline
SuspectFull.relationship: Approves and signs cycle-count adjustments for the warehouse
SuspectFull.motive: Maya’s performance is judged on keeping cycle-count variances low before audits, and she’s been under pressure to keep the nightly adjustment flow moving without delays. If an adjustment later turned out to be improper, she could be motivated to protect her reputation by standing by the approval and minimizing questions about the process.
SuspectFull.alibi: She states she was off the warehouse floor and handling approvals remotely from home after 01:00, and her sent email header for “Re: Cycle Count 3/18 approvals” shows MAYA.K sent an approval message at 01:22:09 with an attached spreadsheet hash logged in the message metadata. The limitation is that this only verifies an email send and attachment version at 01:22, not her location or any later access to the shared drive file.
SuspectFull.background:
Maya is the night shift inventory control lead responsible for reviewing and signing cycle-count adjustments before they are posted in the WMS.

She regularly uses the warehouse email system for approvals and is familiar with the shared-drive spreadsheets used for nightly variance and adjustment workflows.

Her name and account appear in the cycle-count approval email chain associated with the 03/18 adjustment paperwork.

SuspectFull.name: Owen Delgado
SuspectFull.relationship: Oversees outbound dock operations that interface with the victim warehouse’s inventory paperwork
SuspectFull.motive: Owen’s performance metrics are tied to on-time departures and clean outbound documentation, and repeated exceptions can trigger write-ups. He had reason to want irregular returns-cage moves or missing paperwork kept from escalating into a visible dock-side problem during audit week.
SuspectFull.alibi: BOL packet scan log shows his supervisor login (ODEL) at the Dock Office kiosk at 08:14:22 and 08:37:05 on 2026-03-18, with no kiosk entries tied to his login between 01:00 and 06:00. This log reflects kiosk use specifically, so it does not capture where he was if he was away from that terminal.
SuspectFull.background:
Owen runs the day-shift outbound floor, including staging lanes and bill-of-lading packet handling at the dock office kiosk.

His role gives him routine access to shipping paperwork flows and authority to direct how pallets are organized for carrier pickup.

He is not scheduled as an overnight office mezzanine user, and the after-hours activity in this case centers on systems and document handling before day shift begins.

SuspectFull.name: Rafael Ibarra
SuspectFull.relationship: After-hours guard assigned to the warehouse site
SuspectFull.motive: He is responsible for keeping after-hours pickups orderly and documented, and a quiet exception pickup that later drew scrutiny could put his contract standing at risk. If pressure came from drivers or site staff to move things along quickly, he would have a personal reason to minimize delays rather than escalate irregularities.
SuspectFull.alibi: He states he was on scheduled duty at the gatehouse from 22:00–06:00, including processing a courier pickup around 04:06; the security roster and gatehouse/dock-area camera motion log can independently confirm his presence at the window during that time. The limitation is that these records show he was on post, not what he entered into the visitor/gate log line-by-line.
SuspectFull.background: Rafael Ibarra is a third-party security contractor assigned to overnight coverage, handling gate checks and logging after-hours vehicle activity. Site records place him on the 22:00–06:00 shift on 2026-03-18. A gate-related record and a separate camera motion log both correspond to activity at the gatehouse window around 04:05–04:08, consistent with him performing routine pickup processing.

sections.heading: STATEMENT OF (Operations Manager)
sections.text:
I am the Operations Manager at Roseway 3PL in Daly City. My responsibilities include oversight of inventory control processes, cycle counts, and escalation of discrepancies to leadership and to our inventory mailbox for reconciliation.

I understand this statement concerns an inventory discrepancy involving SKU **HHS-4102 (handheld scanners)** and the overnight inventory adjustment workflow, including the period around the **03:00–04:00** window when adjustments are commonly posted and reconciled.

sections.heading: Oath / Affirmation
sections.text: I declare under penalty of perjury that the foregoing is true and correct to the best of my knowledge. I understand that making a false statement may subject me to criminal penalties.

sections.heading: Overnight controls and why the 03:00–04:00 window matters
sections.text:
On our night operations flow, cycle count variances and adjustments are typically assembled and reviewed before they are posted in the WMS. There is an operational sensitivity to the **03:00–04:00** period because that is when the warehouse transitions toward the end-of-shift close-out and when automated posting/processing windows are expected.

In practice, discrepancies that are not addressed before that window can roll into day-shift reconciliation and stand out, while activity during that window can appear routine unless it is cross-checked against supporting documentation and file/version history.

sections.heading: Observed reconciliation reference to HHS-4102 variance

items.label: Adjustment batch referenced in thread
items.value: 03:12 adjustment batch (time as referenced in the thread)

sections.heading: What I recall about approvals and version timing (context)
sections.text:
I am aware the inventory control lead on nights may approve cycle count adjustments by email. In this instance, I was shown header details for an approval email thread titled **“Re: Cycle Count 3/18 approvals”** indicating **Message-ID <cc0318-approval@warehouse.local>** sent from **MAYA.K** at **2026-03-18 01:22:09**.

I was also shown documentation indicating the approved attachment referenced in that email carried a **SHA256 hash beginning “9b1d...e20f”**, while the shared-drive version later associated with the process carried a different **SHA256 hash beginning “4c7a...19d2”** recorded at **2026-03-18 03:15:02** by file server audit.

I cannot personally compute those hashes; I am describing what was presented to me as the header and audit details. The difference in hashes indicates the attachment version referenced at 01:22:09 is not the same as the shared-drive version recorded at 03:15:02.

sections.heading: Operational note (as stated by witness)
sections.text: A later change to a shared-drive spreadsheet after an approval email is possible in our environment if someone has access to the file and saves a new version, even if the approval email itself was legitimately sent earlier.

sections.heading: Documented observations
sections.text: - A reconciliation email thread dated 2026-03-18 references SKU HHS-4102 'handheld scanners' showing a -48 unit variance after the 03:12 adjustment batch.

sections.heading: Suspicion indicators
sections.text: - As inventory control lead, Maya's approval authority could allow her to legitimize an improper cycle-count adjustment.

AssetFull.body:
Photorealistic CCTV still frame from a fixed ceiling corner camera in a warehouse mezzanine office corridor at night. Cool fluorescent lighting, slight green tint, visible digital noise and compression artifacts, with a black timestamp overlay at the bottom reading: “2026-03-18 02:49:02”. The corridor is narrow with beige walls, gray industrial carpet tiles, and a red EXIT sign glowing at the far end. On the right side of frame, a metal door with a small wired-glass window is clearly labeled with a printed placard: “MZ-Office”. Next to the doorframe is a badge reader with a small LED. A single person (gender not clearly identifiable due to motion blur and hood up) is captured mid-step near the badge reader, wearing a dark hoodie under a high-visibility safety vest, carrying a slim folder or clipboard; face partially obscured by the hood brim and camera angle. Include a thin on-screen system overlay box in the upper-left corner as if from the security software, showing readable text: “Event: Door MZ-Office” and “Badge ID: 004982” and “Log ref: TRN-L”. In the lower-right corner, include a small inset note panel (like an operator annotation) with readable text: “BOL kiosk user ‘ODEL’ activity recorded 08:14:22 and 08:37:05 (no entries 01:00–06:00)”—presented as a neutral side note, not a conclusion. Composition: wide-angle lens distortion, straight-on view down the corridor, subject right of center, door label and badge reader sharply visible, overall mood quiet and after-hours.

Briefing.subject: Assignment Briefing — Roseway 3PL “Missing Pallet Ledger” (Inventory Diversion / Cycle Count Manipulation)
Briefing.body:
Det. Ruiz,

Roseway 3PL in Daly City has reported a suspected inventory diversion tied to routine cycle-count activity. Records indicate an overnight WMS adjustment was made to a specific pallet (PLT-77431, tablets), and the pallet was subsequently reported “not located” during follow-up review. The working theory is that ordinary systems and a procedural gap were used to mask product removal.

What we can place on record at this stage: verified WMS audit activity reflects an inventory adjustment (audit token ADJ-920771) during the overnight window, and access-control logs place an employee badge assigned to Alina Cho entering through the employee entrance and using the admin corridor door around the same timeframe. In addition, the “Discrepancy Summary” spreadsheet distributed by the inventory mailbox later that morning shows file metadata indicating it was modified during the overnight hours and saved under the “acho” user.

What remains uncertain is whether the digital activity corresponds to a single operator versus credential/shared-session use, and how the pallet physically left controlled inventory (e.g., through dock/returns handling, standard outbound paperwork, or another pathway). While other personnel have roles that could touch labels, staging, or security rounds, currently available records do not independently establish their involvement in the overnight adjustment or document edits.

This matters now because the loss was initially concealed as routine cycle counts and only surfaced on reconciliation, increasing the risk of further diversion if the same gap remains in place. Immediate objective: secure and correlate the access-control exports, WMS audit trail, and the email/attachment metadata into a clear attribution timeline, then identify the most likely physical egress path for PLT-77431 so we can request targeted preservation from Roseway (dock/returns movement documentation and related logs) before routine retention cycles overwrite them.

Explanation: Linh Tran badged in after hours, entered the mezzanine office, and used the shared workstation to alter the cycle-count adjustment spreadsheet at 03:06 so the HHS-4102 handheld scanners would be written down and reclassified as returns/damaged. Minutes later, an adjustment batch posted at 03:12 from terminal MZ-PC-03, and a courier pickup was logged at Bay 2 at 04:06, consistent with the pallet being physically removed under the weaker returns-exception lane. Two independent trails converge on Linh: the access logs place her badge at Door E-Staff and the MZ-Office during the relevant window, and the shared-drive file properties show the spreadsheet was last modified by LINH.T at the key time. The decisive analysis ties the MZ-PC-03 session artifacts (LINH.T Windows logon and the WMS session token timestamped just before the 03:12 post) to the same machine used for the adjustment, bridging identity, location, and system action—while noting the forensic limitation that endpoint artifacts correlate a session/device and time, not the operator’s hands with absolute certainty. The strongest red herrings fall away: Maya’s “approval” email referenced an earlier attachment hash, indicating the file was changed after she signed off, and Owen’s dock-kiosk log activity begins hours later, missing the overnight window. Rafael’s presence at the gatehouse explains the logged pickup but doesn’t connect him to the mezzanine access, file edit, or WMS adjustment that made the pallet disappear on paper.
